findings.claim: Unauthenticated public ingress can exercise the workload identity
findings.evidence: Task 10 still enables public network access and explicitly specifies no App Service Authentication or IP restrictions. Security Configuration repeats public_edge_auth=none. The same app receives id-web, with Storage Blob Data Contributor, Service Bus Data Sender and Receiver, and Key Vault Secrets User permissions. Requirements assigns end-user authentication to B06/B10, but the current plan does not make an enforced application-layer authorization boundary a prerequisite for deploying the real image or claiming its readiness. Task 13 tests anonymous HTTP 200 responses, not rejection of unauthenticated requests to protected operations. The initial placeholder does not itself demonstrate unauthorized data access; the unresolved exposure is the planned public application boundary when identity-backed operations are introduced.
findings.impact: Once the application exposes operations using these bindings, anonymous Internet callers could invoke those operations with the application's data-plane privileges. Private endpoints and managed-identity authentication protect the app-to-service connection, not authorization of the originating caller.
findings.artifact_section: Implementation Tasks -> Task 10: modules/web.bicep; Code-Generation Contract; Security Configuration

suggested_fix.proposed_edit: Require App Service authentication or an explicitly contracted and enforced B06/B10 application-layer authentication and authorization boundary before identity-backed operations become reachable. Specify which routes may remain anonymous, narrow data-plane grants to required operations, and add negative readiness tests proving anonymous callers cannot invoke protected operations. If the placeholder remains anonymous, distinguish its limited startup test from authorization readiness of the real application. Update Task 10, the app and role-binding contracts, Task 13, and Security Configuration consistently.

findings.claim: The shared Graph-reader identity can be attached outside SQL MI
findings.evidence: The Overview and Task 9 retain the shared B08-owned id-sqlmi-directory as SQL MI's primary user-assigned identity. Task 12 steps 7 and 10 retain Managed Identity Operator for the deploying member on that identity, alongside Owner on the workload subscription. Step 10 explicitly acknowledges that attachment is not restricted to SQL MI and that the identity has User.Read.All, GroupMember.Read.All and Application.Read.All. Its existence and assign/action checks establish attachability, not containment. The updated lifecycle explanation and historical acceptance expressly do not claim implemented attachment controls. The supplied IaC contract preserves this same binding and permission model.
findings.impact: A member controlling another compatible workload resource can attach the shared identity and obtain application-permission Graph access outside SQL MI. This exposes tenant directory data through a reusable, non-SQL workload identity rather than a SQL-MI-bound permission boundary.
findings.artifact_section: Overview -> SQL MI directory identity; Implementation Tasks -> Task 12 steps 7 and 10; Code-Generation Contract -> SQL MI

suggested_fix.proposed_edit: Select a SQL-MI-bound directory identity design, such as granting the necessary Graph permissions to the MI's system-assigned identity through the responsible platform owner, or specify an enforceable and verified restriction preventing members from attaching the Graph-enabled UAMI elsewhere. Update the Overview, Task 9 identity configuration, Task 12 permission checks, SQL MI contract, Security Configuration and machine-readable capability contract together. Do not substitute historical acceptance, identity existence, assign/action permission or unimplemented lifecycle obligations for containment evidence.

findings.claim: Diagnostics readiness does not prove required metrics coverage
findings.evidence: The six archetype-owned settings remain metrics-only on the storage account, four private endpoints and App Service plan. The plan delegates diagnostics for App Service, ACR, Service Bus, Key Vault, SQL MI, Application Insights and Blob service to DINE, while Task 13 step 6 checks setting presence and workspace targeting rather than enabled categories and metrics. The supplied governance records contain assignment parameters, not deployment templates proving complete coverage. Several assignments specify categoryGroup=audit without demonstrating metrics coverage. Importantly, the Blob service assignment does specify metricsEnabled=true and logsEnabled=true, so the prior assertion that none of the seven policies configures metrics is not supported. Nevertheless, the six other service targets lack demonstrated metrics coverage, and the readiness test does not validate the Blob setting's actual contents either. The contract's generic metric_categories=[AllMetrics] is not a per-target implementation mapping.
findings.impact: Readiness can pass despite missing service metrics or required log categories, reducing visibility into failed requests, resource exhaustion and service degradation. A setting's existence does not establish compliance with the logs-and-metrics baseline.
findings.artifact_section: Governance Compliance Matrix -> DINE resource logs; Implementation Tasks -> Tasks 3-10 and Task 13; Security Configuration -> Diagnostics

suggested_fix.proposed_edit: Enumerate supported required logs and metrics for all thirteen diagnostic targets. Establish which categories policy actually supplies, including Blob's metricsEnabled setting, and explicitly provide missing metrics without duplicating policy-owned logs. Extend readiness checks to inspect the expected destination, enabled log categories/category groups and metric categories for each target. Replace the generic contract declaration with an unambiguous per-target ownership and coverage mapping.

findings.claim: Deployment phases are labels, not independent recovery boundaries
findings.evidence: Deployment Phases still mandates one azd provision and one subscription-scope ARM deployment, with no phase parameter or independent split. Its foundation, security/data and compute phases have no intermediate deployment gates; Task 1 allows independent branches to run concurrently. Failure and recovery correctly acknowledges that ARM does not roll back and that a partially created SQL MI remains billable, but recovery remains fixing the cause and rerunning the full deployment. There is no bounded retry/escalation procedure or explicit disposition of a still-running SQL MI branch. The owner instruction to use one deployment is a constraint, not evidence that this recovery risk has been technically addressed.
findings.impact: A late or repeated provisioning failure can leave a partially deployed, billable stack without an independently validated resume point. Repeated full-deployment attempts increase diagnosis time and unresolved SQL MI cost.

suggested_fix.proposed_edit: Prefer independently validated deployment boundaries with defined outputs, prerequisites and resume behavior. If the one-deployment constraint remains, describe these sections as dependency stages rather than recovery boundaries and document the risk justification plus a bounded recovery procedure: inspect nested operations and SQL MI state, distinguish in-progress from failed operations, define when to wait or retry, cap retries and name the escalation/stop condition. Preserve separate human authorization for cancellation or cleanup and explicitly account for SQL MI billing while blocked.
